newsitem.title: UK: China's HK General perfect choice, says tutor.
newsitem.headline: China's HK General perfect choice, says tutor.

text.p: The Chinese General who led Beijing's troops into Hong Kong is the perfect choice for one of the most sensitive military posts in Asia, one of his old tutors at a British defence college said on Tuesday.
Major-General Zhou Borong was the first officer from China's People's Liberation Army (PLA) to attend the Royal College of Defence Studies where he was one of the stars of the Class of 1988.
He led the 40-strong advance guard which arrived in Hong Kong this week on Queen Elizabeth's 71st birthday to oversee the handover of the British colony to China at the end of June.
"I think he is a remarkably astute choice," said Major-General John Evans, one of his tutors at the college which attracts military officers from around the world for its geo-political courses.

"Even in 1988 he appeared to be the perfect choice for a senior officer in such a sensitive appointment as Hong Kong after its handover to China and I am delighted he has been given that appointment," Evans told Reuters.
"He was a very high grade man, there were no flies on him. He could genuinely hold his own," Evans added.

Zhou joined a year-long course with senior officers from about 20 countries at the college, set up after World War One at the instigation of Winston Churchill to widen the political horizons of military officers.
He lived in British Army quarters in London with his wife who came to the British capital knowing only about three words of English but who left with a solid linguistic grounding.
"He was thrown into a capitalist society from a communist background. It must have been extraordinarily difficult and strange for him and he proved to be very personable," Evans said.
Zhou, 52, will need acute political antennae in the countdown to the handover.
His unarmed contingent staged a low-key arrival in the colony with no pomp and little ceremony to mark the beginning of the end for a century and a half of British rule.
The advance PLA party will live alongside the remaining British soldiers in the Prince of Wales barracks and at a naval base on nearby Stonecutters Island.
But few in Hong Kong expect to see the Chinese relaxing in Hong Kong's bars or nightclubs with British troops and American sailors from U.S. warships visiting the port.
Evans was fulsome in praise of Zhou, saying: "His great virtues are that he understands western society. His personality combines intelligence and humour and the ability to get on with people."

But he stressed: "I would never question his loyalty. He didn't go native. There was never any doubt that he was anything but a loyal Chinese officer. He contributed the Chinese point of view but had the gift of doing it with humour."
"He had never lived, worked and mixed in western society before and he did it brilliantly. At the end of the year he quite genuinely had our respect and affection," he said.
